newsitem.title: UK: Gloom lifts for BA as caterers seek talks.
newsitem.headline: Gloom lifts for BA as caterers seek talks.

text.p: Tension eased at British Airways on Monday afternoon after one group of unions in dispute with the airline agreed to seek talks rather than call for a walkout over the sale of its catering division.

BA, Europe's biggest carrier, has been fighting an industrial relations war on two fronts since last month, resulting in much sabre-rattling and, analysts estimate, tens of millions of pounds in lost bookings and costs as passengers have switched to rival carriers.
BA ran a skeleton service last week during a 72-hour strike by cabin crew over pay and conditions.

The caterers' decision was good news for BA as a strike would almost certainly have dragged in baggage handlers and check-in staff during the heavy holiday travelling season. BA spokesman, Michael Blunt, called it "a welcome result"
However the main dispute facing BA, involving cabin crew, is yet to be resolved. Flights are still being affected even though the walkout ended on Friday.

Cabin crew leaders, members of the same union which represents the caterers, are meeting on Monday to draw up alternative proposals for achieving 42 million pounds ($71 million) worth of savings being sought by BA's chief executive Bob Ayling.
A union spokesman told Reuters the most recent sticking point for cabin crew talks -- BA's threat to suspend flight attendants who went on strike last week -- had been resolved.
BA has denied that any employee was being punished, but noted that some would have to wait to be rostered while airline operations got back to normal.
Talks between the two sides are likely to go ahead later this week after BA has studied the union proposals.
And with the catering spat close to resolution, the threat to BA of a 'double-whammy' of strikes in the future appeared to be receding -- for now.

The caterers would need to hold another ballot if they wanted to organise a walkout in the future. Unions are obliged to take action within 28 days of a strike ballot and must give the company seven-days notice, a T&G union spokesman said.

"Our representatives concluded that the best way forward is to seek fresh negotiations with BA over the concerns about the catering sell-off," George Ryde, the senior civil aviation officer at the Transport and General Workers' Union (T&G) told the UK Press Association news agency.
The 1,400 catering workers, members of the T&G, last week rejected company proposals aimed at protecting their terms and conditions after the sale of the catering unit.
The sale is part of the airline's overall drive to sharpen its competitiveness by saving around one billion pounds by 2000 in several areas of its business.
Following the cabin crew walkout, which started last Wednesday and ended Saturday, BA said normal service on its worldwide network would not resume until mid-week.
"We're hoping to restore a full programme (of flights) by mid-week," a BA spokeswoman told Reuters.
She said flight problems were exacerbated by the fact that out of 2,000 cabin crew who called in sick last week only 200 had so far reported in for work.

BA however says it will not sue or dismiss strikers as it had threatened last week -- but they still risked losing travel perks, promotion and severance opportunities. They were also being asked for an assurance that they were prepared to work normally.
BA today ran 74 out of its 122 European flights from London Heathrow airport, 41 out of 48 daily long-haul flights and 32 out of 60 domestic services.
($ = 0.591 British Pounds)
